newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - UK data point to steady interest rates.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - UK data point to steady interest rates.

text.p: British manufacturing expanded modestly in February and money supply growth slowed, according to figures published on Monday which made it increasingly likely that the government will leave interest rates unchanged.

The Chartered Institute of Purchasing and Supply (CIPS) said its purchasing managers' index (PMI) dipped slightly to a seasonally adjusted 53.5 from 53.9 in January, pointing to a very slight easing in the rate of manufacturing growth.
"Output recorded the fastest growth since November 1994 as firms cleared backlogs of orders and rebuilt stocks of finished goods," it said.
The PMI is seen as a reliable barometer of activity in industry.
The Bank of England said M0 money supply, a narrow measure of money supply, grew a provisional 6.5 percent in the year to February, down from 7.3 percent year-on-year in January.
The slowdown in the growth rate was welcome news for finance minister Kenneth Clarke, who has been resisting pressure from the Bank of England to raise interest rates from their present 6.0 percent.
The Bank has expressed concern about the economy beginning to overheat and argues that rising money supply may be a pointer to a future upsurge in inflation.

"The figures suggest that consumers may have just eased off the accelerator in the last couple of months, perhaps due to uncertainties over the likely course of interest rates after the general election," said Jonathan Loynes, an economist at HSBC Markets.
But he noted that M0 remained well outside the government's monitoring range of zero to four percent.

Clarke, the Chancellor of the Exchequer, meets Bank of England Governor Eddie George for their monthly monetary meeting on Wednesday. Most economists expect Clarke, who has the final say on monetary policy, to leave rates unchanged.
Raising interest rates would mean dearer home loans for millions of Britons and would make the Conservative government even more unpopular in the run-up to the election, which is due by May.
The PMI survey showed domestic orders remained buoyant but export orders grew only modestly as the strong pound made it more difficult for British firms to sell their goods abroad.
"The increasing strength of the pound, by making UK goods more expensive in overseas markets, was increasingly being blamed for lost orders," the CIPS said.
However, the strong pound did benefit producers in the form of reduced import prices. Overall input prices fell for the 16th consecutive month in February.

Loynes said that while the prices index showed the outlook for inflation was excellent, the strong pound would make life more difficult for manufacturers this year. "With the worst of the impact of sterling's huge appreciation still to come, the outlook for manufacturers in 1997 is far from rosy," he said. "Mr Clarke is well justified in leaving interest rates on hold."
